Treating a rating scale as continuous

Source: vignettes/ordinal-or-continuous.qmd
ordinal-or-continuous.Rmd
library(ctsem)
library(ggplot2)

A rating scale can be modelled in two ways in ctsem. manifesttype = 0 treats the observed code as continuous with a Gaussian residual, and manifesttype = 2 uses a cumulative logit. Ordinal indicators require backend = 'julia'. The other indicator types are covered in the measurement models vignette.

To see what the choice changes, we simulate from a known process, categorise it, and fit the same dynamic model both ways. A single simulated sample has its own sampling error, so each comparison with the generating values below is shown with its uncertainty, and a fit does well when its interval covers the true value.

Code that only generates data or draws figures is folded. Unfold it to reproduce the figures.

The data

Two Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes, one five point item each. eta1 affects eta2 and not the reverse, the innovations correlate at 0.4, people differ moderately in where their processes sit, and four thresholds at ±1\pm1 and ±2.8\pm2.8 cut each process into categories.

Code

DRIFT <- matrix(c(-0.5, 0,
                  0.3, -0.5), 2, 2, byrow = TRUE)   # eta1 -> eta2 is 0.3
diffsd <- 2.2
diffcor <- 0.4
thresholds <- c(-2.8, -1.0, 1.0, 2.8)

# covmattransform='z' makes a covariance matrix's off-diagonal exactly
# atanh(correlation), so the generating values can be written down.
zmat <- function(sd1, sd2, r) matrix(c(sd1, 0, atanh(r), sd2), 2, 2, byrow = TRUE)

# Stationary covariance, solving A S + S A' + Q = 0: its standard deviations
# are what the true standardised cross effect is scaled by.
Q <- diag(diffsd, 2) %*% matrix(c(1, diffcor, diffcor, 1), 2) %*% diag(diffsd, 2)
S <- matrix(solve(kronecker(diag(2), DRIFT) + kronecker(DRIFT, diag(2)),
  -as.vector(Q)), 2, 2)
latentsd <- sqrt(diag(S))

gen <- ctModel(type = 'ct', n.latent = 2, n.manifest = 2,
  manifestNames = c('eta1', 'eta2'), latentNames = c('eta1', 'eta2'),
  LAMBDA = diag(1, 2), DRIFT = DRIFT,
  DIFFUSION = zmat(diffsd, diffsd, diffcor),
  T0VAR = diag(1,2),
  T0MEANS = matrix(1, 2, 1), CINT = matrix(0, 2, 1),
  MANIFESTMEANS = matrix(0, 2, 1),
  MANIFESTVAR = diag(1e-6, 2),          # no measurement error: manifest = state
  Tpoints = 30)
gen$covmattransform <- 'z'

# backend='julia' because the R generator reads DIFFUSION and T0VAR as square
# roots whatever covmattransform says, while the julia generator applies the
# declared transform, as ctFit() does.
set.seed(2)
d <- data.frame(ctGenerate(gen, n = 150, Tpoints = 30, dtmean = 0.7,
  backend = 'julia'))

# The cumulative logit: the response falls in category k or below when the
# state plus a logistic disturbance is below threshold k.
ordinalise <- function(eta)
  1 + rowSums(outer(eta + rlogis(length(eta)), thresholds, '>'))
# Moderate individual differences: each person's process sits a little high or
# low. Added to the states, before they are categorised.
set.seed(3)
shift <- matrix(stats::rnorm(150 * 2, 0, 0.8), 150, 2)
d$eta1 <- d$eta1 + shift[d$id, 1]
d$eta2 <- d$eta2 + shift[d$id, 2]

set.seed(502)
d$y1 <- ordinalise(d$eta1)
d$y2 <- ordinalise(d$eta2)

One subject. The line is the latent process, the dotted lines are the thresholds, and the points are the recorded answers at the middle of the band each category stands for:

Code

mid <- c(-3.8, -1.9, 0, 1.9, 3.8)             # band midpoints, for display
s <- d[d$id == 1, ]

ggplot(s, aes(time)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = thresholds, linetype = 3, colour = 'grey55') +
  geom_line(aes(y = eta1, colour = 'latent eta1')) +
  geom_point(aes(y = mid[y1], colour = 'recorded category y1'), size = 1.9) +
  scale_y_continuous(sec.axis = sec_axis(~., breaks = mid, labels = 1:5,
    name = 'category')) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c('latent eta1' = 'grey35',
    'recorded category y1' = '#c0392b')) +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = 'bottom') +
  labs(x = 'time', y = 'latent scale', colour = NULL)

The points follow the line, but only to the resolution of the bands, and they cross a threshold early or late depending on the noise. Both items use the whole scale, and no category is very rare:

Code

freq <- rbind(data.frame(item = 'y1', category = factor(d$y1)),
  data.frame(item = 'y2', category = factor(d$y2)))

ggplot(freq, aes(category)) + geom_bar() + facet_wrap(~item) +
  theme_bw() + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)

Fitting it as ordinal

Two arguments make an indicator ordinal. manifesttype = 2 asks for the cumulative logit, and ncategories gives the number of categories, so that the model knows how many thresholds to estimate before it sees the data.

ordinalmodel <- ctModel(type = 'ct', n.latent = 2, n.manifest = 2,
  manifestNames = c('y1', 'y2'), latentNames = c('eta1', 'eta2'),
  manifesttype = c(2, 2),             # ordinal
  ncategories = c(5, 5),              # five point scale
  LAMBDA = diag(1, 2))

ordinalfit <- ctFit(d[, c('id', 'time', 'y1', 'y2')], ordinalmodel,
  backend = 'julia')

Everything else is left at its default. CINT is zero by default, so the process mean is in T0MEANS, which is estimated and varies over people. So does MANIFESTMEANS, which gives each person their own level and their own item locations. ctFit() fixes MANIFESTVAR to zero for binary and ordinal indicators, because the cumulative logit already supplies the randomness and a residual variance would not be identified.

ncategories when the indicators are mixed

ncategories takes one entry per manifest variable, or a single value for all of them, and only the ordinal entries are read. For a model with a Gaussian, an ordinal and a binary indicator, these three are equivalent:

ncategories = c(NA, 5, NA)    # NA where it does not apply
ncategories = c(0, 5, 0)      # or zero
ncategories = 5               # or one value, since the rest are ignored

NA is the clearest of the three, because it shows that the number does not apply to that variable. Values for variables that are not ordinal are set to zero. If any variable is ordinal and ncategories is missing, ctsem stops with an error that names the variables.

summary() reports the thresholds on the latent scale, one row per category boundary:

summary(ordinalfit)$thresholds
#>          mean    sd   2.5%    50%  97.5%
#> y1 1|2 -3.046 0.186 -3.414 -3.047 -2.688
#> y1 2|3 -1.150 0.127 -1.412 -1.154 -0.903
#> y1 3|4  0.969 0.116  0.749  0.972  1.185
#> y1 4|5  2.876 0.168  2.540  2.885  3.216
#> y2 1|2 -3.171 0.192 -3.542 -3.181 -2.789
#> y2 2|3 -1.213 0.157 -1.524 -1.218 -0.903
#> y2 3|4  0.838 0.150  0.551  0.835  1.140
#> y2 4|5  2.716 0.174  2.376  2.717  3.054

The generating values were −2.8, −1, 1 and 2.8.

Fitting it as continuous

The Gaussian version is the same call with manifesttype = 0, no ncategories, and a free residual variance per item instead of thresholds:

gaussianmodel <- ctModel(type = 'ct', n.latent = 2, n.manifest = 2,
  manifestNames = c('y1', 'y2'), latentNames = c('eta1', 'eta2'),
  LAMBDA = diag(1, 2))

gaussianfit <- ctFit(d[, c('id', 'time', 'y1', 'y2')], gaussianmodel,
  backend = 'julia')

What should and should not agree

The two fits put the latent processes on different scales. In both, LAMBDA is fixed at 1, so the latent process takes its units from the indicator. The Gaussian fit therefore measures eta1 in answer codes, and the ordinal fit in logits, since the scale of the cumulative logit is fixed.

The link function sets this scale, and the thresholds would rescale along with the process. With the loadings free as well, nothing sets the scale, which is the identification problem covered in the item response vignette.

A parameter can therefore only be compared across the two fits if it is invariant to rescaling the latent processes.

Expected to agree

  • Auto effects (drift_eta1, drift_eta2). Their unit is inverse time, and a rate of reversion does not change when the process is measured in other units.
  • The diffusion correlation, being a correlation.
  • The standardised cross effect, the effect in stationary standard deviations, ã21=a21sd(η1)/sd(η2)\tilde{a}_{21} = a_{21}\,\text{sd}(\eta_1)/\text{sd}(\eta_2).

Not expected to agree

  • The raw cross effect drift_eta2_eta1, whose unit is eta2 per unit of eta1 per unit time. The same holds within one fit. eta2 is more variable because it accumulates eta1, so the same effect takes different values on processes with different scales.
  • DIFFUSION and T0VAR on their own, and the residual variances.
  • MANIFESTMEANS, a location on the latent scale in the Gaussian fit and the thresholds’ anchor in the ordinal one.

Only the ordinal fit’s scale has a meaning outside the questionnaire, so where the raw quantities differ, report the ordinal fit.

Comparison

ctDiscretePars() turns each fit’s DRIFT into the regressions it implies at every time interval, once per draw from the fit’s uncertainty. Standardised, those are comparable across the two fits. The line is the median over draws, the band holds 95% of them, and the dashed line is the generating process:

Code

times <- seq(0, 6, .1)

crossband <- function(fit, label) {
  a <- ctDiscretePars(fit, times = times, standardise = TRUE,
    nsamples = 500)[, 1, , 2, 1]                 # draws x intervals, eta1 -> eta2
  data.frame(time = times, model = label,
    median = apply(a, 2, median, na.rm = TRUE),
    lo = apply(a, 2, quantile, .025, na.rm = TRUE),
    hi = apply(a, 2, quantile, .975, na.rm = TRUE))
}

bands <- rbind(crossband(gaussianfit, 'gaussian on the codes'),
  crossband(ordinalfit, 'ordinal'))
truth <- data.frame(time = times, value = sapply(times,
  function(u) expm::expm(DRIFT * u)[2, 1] * latentsd[1] / latentsd[2]))

ggplot(bands, aes(time)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = 'grey82') +
  geom_line(aes(y = median, colour = 'estimate', linetype = 'estimate'),
    linewidth = .9) +
  geom_line(data = truth, aes(y = value, colour = 'truth', linetype = 'truth'),
    linewidth = .9) +
  facet_wrap(~ model) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(estimate = 'grey15', truth = '#c0392b')) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c(estimate = 1, truth = 2)) +
  theme_bw() + theme(legend.position = 'bottom') +
  labs(x = 'time interval', y = 'standardised cross effect, eta1 -> eta2',
    colour = NULL, linetype = NULL)

The auto effect, the stationary standard deviation of eta1 and the diffusion correlation come from the same draws, through ctExtract(): pop_DRIFT, pop_asymDIFFUSIONcov, the stationary covariance the model implies, and pop_DIFFUSIONcov, the innovation covariance. Each cell is the median with a 95% interval:

Code

comparable <- function(fit, label) {
  e <- ctExtract(fit)
  q <- e$pop_DIFFUSIONcov
  draws <- cbind(drift_eta1 = e$pop_DRIFT[, 1, 1],
    latentsd1 = sqrt(e$pop_asymDIFFUSIONcov[, 1, 1]),
    diffcor = q[, 1, 2] / sqrt(q[, 1, 1] * q[, 2, 2]))
  s <- apply(draws, 2, quantile, c(.5, .025, .975))
  out <- data.frame(label, t(sprintf('%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]', s[1, ], s[2, ], s[3, ])))
  setNames(out, c('model', colnames(draws)))
}

knitr::kable(rbind(comparable(gaussianfit, 'gaussian on the codes'),
  comparable(ordinalfit, 'ordinal'),
  data.frame(model = 'truth', drift_eta1 = sprintf('%.2f', DRIFT[1, 1]),
    latentsd1 = sprintf('%.2f', latentsd[1]), diffcor = sprintf('%.2f', diffcor))))
model drift_eta1 latentsd1 diffcor
gaussian on the codes -0.57 [-0.77, -0.42] 0.98 [0.91, 1.04] 0.37 [0.22, 0.48]
ordinal -0.57 [-0.77, -0.42] 2.34 [2.00, 2.67] 0.38 [0.24, 0.50]
truth -0.50 2.20 0.40

latentsd1 is in answer-code units for the Gaussian fit and in logits for the ordinal fit, so the two fitted values cannot be compared with each other. The ordinal value can be compared with the true value, because the link fixes its units, and it is worth checking first.

In both fits, every interval in the table that should cover its generating value does. The bands mostly agree too. The Gaussian band covers the true curve throughout, while from an interval of about one and a half the true curve runs along the upper edge of the ordinal band. Both estimated curves are below the truth by similar amounts, which is what sampling error shared by two fits of the same sample looks like.

In this design the Gaussian approximation costs little for the quantities that do not depend on scale. Given the latent state, categorisation is a monotone transformation plus noise that is independent across items and occasions, and a Gaussian residual can absorb much of that. The other quantities differ in meaning. The Gaussian fit’s raw effects, variances and locations describe the answer codes of this questionnaire, while the ordinal fit’s are on the scale fixed by the link, and those are the ones to report.
